title: Retention Loops Beat Growth Hacks
transcript:
Jordan Vance: Dana, you've been vocal that most so-called growth hacks are actually just acquisition tricks that don't compound. What do you mean by that?

Dana Okonkwo-Reyes: A growth hack, in the pejorative sense, is a one-time clever move. You get a wave of signups from a viral tweet or a clever referral incentive, and then the wave passes and your baseline growth rate is exactly where it was before. A growth loop is different because the output of one cycle becomes the input of the next cycle, so it compounds instead of decaying. Referral programs can be loops if designed right, but most of them aren't, they're just a discount code.

Jordan Vance: What makes a referral program an actual loop versus just a discount code?

Dana Okonkwo-Reyes: The loop only works if using the product itself naturally produces the referral action, and if the referred user becomes a new source of the same behavior. Take a scheduling tool where every meeting invite includes a branded link. The core usage of the product, scheduling meetings, automatically creates exposure to new people. Those new people book a meeting, some fraction of them become users, and now they're sending invites too. Compare that to a generic give-ten-get-ten banner sitting in a settings page nobody visits. Both are technically referral programs. Only one is a loop, because only one is structurally tied to the core action of the product.

Jordan Vance: How do you identify where a loop could exist in a product that doesn't have one yet?

Dana Okonkwo-Reyes: I look for any point where a single user's action creates an artifact that other people see or receive. A shared document, an invoice, a public profile, a piece of exported content, a notification to a non-user. Each of those is a potential loop seed. Then I ask three questions. Does using the product normally create this artifact, without asking the user to do extra work? Does the artifact reach people who aren't already users? And is there a low-friction path from seeing the artifact to becoming a user themselves. If all three are true, you likely have a loop you can strengthen. If you have to bolt on a share button that doesn't fit the natural workflow, you're forcing a loop that won't compound.

Jordan Vance: What's a common mistake teams make once they've found a real loop?

Dana Okonkwo-Reyes: They measure the wrong thing. They'll track total shares or total invites sent as a vanity metric, when the number that actually matters is the loop's cycle time and its conversion rate at each step, because that's what determines whether the loop is accelerating or decaying. A loop with a thirty-day cycle time and forty percent step conversion behaves completely differently than one with a three-day cycle time and ten percent conversion, even if the total shares look similar in a monthly report.

Jordan Vance: If someone is starting from zero this week, what's the first move?

Dana Okonkwo-Reyes: Map every artifact your product already produces as a side effect of normal use, before you invent anything new. Most products already have two or three of these sitting unused. The fastest wins come from removing friction on an existing natural artifact, not from inventing a brand new incentive program from scratch.
